query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys outside the well-studied Nb-Ta and titanium-rich systems is governed by the combination of high configurational entropy, localized pockets of nonrandom atomic distributions (clustered ordering), and the type of mobile dislocations present in the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid solution with at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each
generation.intervention: Introduction of varying concentrations of elements to create high-entropy alloys with different microstructures and dislocation types
generation.conditions: Low temperature regime, with a focus on the role of edge dislocations and clustered ordering on superconducting properties
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructure, including the formation of solid solution phases, intermetallic compounds, and the presence of edge or screw dislocations
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of mixing stabilizes solid solution phases and suppresses the formation of intermetallic phases, while localized pockets of nonrandom atomic distributions and edge dislocations contribute to the enhancement of mechanical properties and potentially superconducting behavior
generation.predicted_outcome: High-entropy alloys with optimized combinations of elements and microstructures will exhibit improved superconducting properties, including higher critical temperatures and upper critical fields
generation.baseline: Conventional superconducting alloys, such as Nb-Ta and titanium-rich systems
generation.boundary: The high-entropy alloy composition and microstructure must be within the defined constraints of at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, and the alloy must be in a solid solution state
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between high configurational entropy, clustered ordering, and edge dislocations on superconducting behavior is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of high-entropy alloy compositions and microstructures to investigate the effects on superconducting properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of high configurational entropy, clustered ordering, and edge dislocations does not lead to improved superconducting properties, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. Moreover, in the case of various ternary Nb-Ti-Hf and Nb-Ti-Ta and quaternary Nb-Ti-Ta-Hf alloys, the highest values of μ0Hc2 were observed for the titanium-rich alloys []. AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations. We use the insight and theory to perform a computationally-guided search over 107 BCC HEAs and identify over 106 possible ultra-strong high-T alloy compositions for future exploration.Subject terms: Mechanical engineering, Mechanical properties, Computational methods The strength in BCC high-entropy alloys is associated with the type of mobile dislocations. The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. Namely, the dependence of Tc on valence electron count (VEC) for HEAs exhibits interesting trends when that was compared with those for classical alloys (metals) and amorphous alloys. Through the proposed methodology, involving high-energy mechanical milling combined with sintering without the application of pressure, it was possible to manufacture high entropy alloys of the CuCrFeNiTiAlx system. Here, the effect of Al on the microstructure, phase evolution, and chemical behavior of the resulting alloys was studied. The following are the main conclusions reached in this study: The powder metallurgy process was proven as an effective experimental route to retain the characteristic microstructure of high entropy alloys. Since milling induces a finer particle size and high lattice distortion, both conditions facilitate metal bonding in the solid state. Furthermore, sintering promotes metal diffusion and, consequently, their solubility and sample densification. Based on the XRD studies, as the Al concentration increases, high entropy alloys undergo a microstructural transformation, from a single FCC phase to a mixture of coexisting phases made of FCC and BCC phases, as well as the precipitation of different compounds such as FeNi, Al3Ni, CrNiFe, TiAl, and Ti3Al.
